### Workflow: keep a character or product the same in every shot (Library, @name, identity sheet, voice)

1. Save one clean picture of them to the Library: **More › Save to Library…** on the picture, or **New {Noun}** on a category page. For a character, an **Identity sheet** helps.
2. Write `@name` in every prompt that shows them. Their picture attaches as a numbered reference; See what gets sent shows the words the model receives.
3. For one look across the film, make a Looks item and write `#name` in each prompt.
4. Give a character a voice (their card → **Add voice**). On video models that take one, the voice attaches with the `@name`.
5. Check the reference rail before pressing **Generate**: a tile marked **Not sent** is past the model's limit.

Details: THE LIBRARY; "Prompt box: @ and # mentions, image 1 citations".

### Library: sheet tools (Identity sheet, Establishing image, turnaround, character sheet, price)
- **Identity sheet**: a portrait plus front and back full-body views of one character.
- **Establishing image**: one clean, empty wide view of a place.
- Every thing can use either tool, whatever its category. A look has none. The picker starts on Identity sheet for Things and Characters items and on Establishing image for Locations items.
- Where: the New dialog's Generate form, **Generate Library Sheet**, and **Generate sheet…** on a card. The result becomes that item's one picture.
- The tools run on the app's default image model; no control picks another. The line **Est. ~{price} for 1 image at {resolution}** shows the price before you confirm, and the run bills the same figure.
- They need an active licence. With no credit route the run says "Out of credits. Add credits in Settings -> Account to keep generating."
- No product sheet exists: for a product or prop, use a clean picture.
- Agent: slates_estimate_generation_cost first, then slates_generate_character_identity or slates_generate_environment_plate with any item's id."}

{"topic":"slates-character-identity","tier":"free","depth":"card","bytes":1899,"guide":"# Character identity sheet — Slates workflow

A character's identity sheet is attached to **every** downstream generation that mentions it, so a flaw in the sheet becomes a flaw in every shot made from it. Building it well is the highest-leverage thing you can do for a project.


> **The general law: the model reads a reference literally.**
> A reference image is not a suggestion. Whatever is baked into it — lighting, medium, texture, symmetry, competing identities — is read as a **property of the subject** and reproduced downstream. A baked rim light tints every shot made from that sheet. A sheet that looks like a 3D game render gets animated like game footage. Two competing renderings of one face get averaged into a third face.

Every reference rule below is a corollary of that one sentence, which is why "prep the reference" beats "prompt around the reference" every time:

- **Flat, plain identity refs** — because scene lighting in the sheet becomes scene lighting in the output (Slates' own receipt: a studio-lit sheet produced a subject that looked green-screen-pasted in front of mountains).
- **One authoritative rendering per subject** — because the model cannot tell which panel is the real one. ByteDance documents this failure directly: multi-view character assets "confuse the model's character recognition, causing it to generate duplicate characters of the same appearance."
- **No 3D-game-render look in a reference** — the model recognizes the render mood and inherits its motion character, so the *animation* comes out looking like game footage. This is not a taste rule

Sections (request with query, or depth "full"):
- Character identity sheet — Slates workflow
- The shape: ONE sheet, three panels
- Workflow
- Get the reference
- Create the character record
- Generate the sheet
- Hand back
- How the reference gets used at scene time
- Anti-patterns"}

To get the same face in every shot, save the character to the **Library** once and then mention them by name in each prompt. Their picture is then sent as a reference with every generation.

### Steps

1. **Put the character in the Library.**
   - If you already have a good picture of them: on that picture, choose **More › Save to Library…**
   - If you're starting from scratch: open the Characters page and click **New Character**.

2. **Make an Identity sheet (recommended).** This is a single image with a portrait plus front and back full-body views. You'll find it under **Generate sheet…** on the character's card, or in the New dialog's Generate form. The cost appears as **Est. ~{price}…** before you confirm.

3. **Write `@name` in every prompt that shows them**, for example: `@Maya walks into the diner`. The character's picture is attached as a numbered reference. To check exactly what the model receives, use **See what gets sent**.

4. **Check the reference rail before pressing Generate.** If a tile says **Not sent**, you've gone past that model's reference limit and the face won't be used. Remove other references to make room.

### Optional
- **Same look across the film:** create a Looks item and put `#name` in each prompt.
- **Same voice:** on the character's card, click **Add voice**. Video models that accept a voice will use it whenever `@name` appears.

### Tips for the reference picture
The model copies whatever is in the reference, so the quality of that picture affects every shot:
- **Use flat, even lighting on a plain background.** If the reference has strong lighting, like a rim light or studio lighting, that lighting shows up in every shot. The character can end up looking pasted onto the scene.
- **Use one image per character.** If you give several different pictures of the same face, the model may blend them into a new face or show the character twice.
- **Avoid a video-game render look** unless you want that style. The animation tends to come out looking like game footage.

I can help you set this up for a character in your current project, such as creating the Library entry or generating the Identity sheet. I'll show you the cost before generating anything.
